16.1.crux: We see an object only when light from it reaches our eyes, either light it makes itself or light it reflects.

cards.title: How we see

steps.text: Light comes from a source like the Sun or a bulb
It falls on an object and bounces off (reflects)
The reflected light enters our eyes, and we see the object

say: In a completely dark room you can't see anything, even with your eyes open.
Light is what makes things visible.
cards.remember: No light reaching your eye = nothing seen.

cards.title: Two kinds of objects

cols.head: Illuminated
cells: Only reflect light falling on them

say: Most objects you see are illuminated: they reflect light from a source.

cards.title: Light bounces
say: When light falls on a surface and bounces back, it is called reflection.

crux_points: We see objects when light from them enters our eyes.
Luminous objects make light; illuminated objects reflect it.
Bouncing back of light from a surface is reflection.

quiz.q: Why can't we see anything in a fully dark room?
options: No light reaches our eyes from objects
quiz.why: We need light from objects to enter our eyes.

quiz.q: The Moon is…
options: Luminous: it makes its own light
quiz.why: The Moon has no light of its own; it reflects sunlight.

16.2.crux: When light reflects from a mirror, the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in the same plane.

cards.title: Parts of a reflection
say: The normal is an imaginary line drawn at right angles to the mirror at the point where the light hits it.
Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror.

cards.title: The two laws
say: Law 1: the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
Law 2: the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.

cards.title: Like a bouncing ball

steps.text: Throw a ball at a slant onto the floor
It bounces off at the same slant on the other side
Light reflecting from a mirror behaves the same way

say: If light hits the mirror straight along the normal, it comes straight back.

crux_points: Incident ray, normal and reflected ray describe a reflection.
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
The incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in one plane.

quiz.q: Which line is marked '?'
quiz.why: The dashed line at 90° to the mirror is the normal.

quiz.q: Light hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 40°. The angle of reflection is…
quiz.why: The angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence.

16.3.crux: A smooth surface like a mirror reflects parallel rays in one direction (regular reflection); a rough surface scatters them in all directions (diffused reflection).

cards.title: Smooth vs rough
say: Parallel rays hitting a smooth surface come back parallel.
On a rough surface, the same rays bounce off in different directions.

cards.title: Laws still hold

steps.text: Zoom in on a rough surface: it has many tiny slopes
At each tiny point, angle of incidence = angle of reflection
But the slopes face different ways, so the rays scatter

say: Diffused reflection is not a failure of the laws of reflection. It's caused by the bumpy surface.

cards.title: Which is which?
say: Diffused reflection lets us see objects from any direction.

crux_points: Regular reflection: smooth surfaces keep parallel rays parallel.
Diffused reflection: rough surfaces scatter the rays.
The laws of reflection hold at every point in both cases.

quiz.q: Light falling on cardboard undergoes…
quiz.why: Cardboard is rough, so it scatters light in all directions.

quiz.q: Do the laws of reflection hold for diffused reflection?
quiz.why: Each tiny part follows the laws; the rough surface makes rays go different ways.

16.4.crux: Reflected light can be reflected again; a periscope uses two mirrors to let you see over or around obstacles.

cards.title: The periscope

labels.name: Bottom mirror
labels.note: At 45°: turns light to your eye

say: Light from the object reflects off the top mirror, travels down the tube, and reflects again off the bottom mirror into your eye.

cards.title: Who uses periscopes?
say: You can make a simple periscope with a long box and two small mirrors.

cards.title: Mirrors in daily life

steps.text: At the barber's, one mirror shows your back
Its image is reflected again in the front mirror
So you can see the back of your head

say: This is reflected light being reflected again.

crux_points: Reflected light can be reflected again by another mirror.
A periscope uses two mirrors at 45°.
Periscopes are used in submarines, tanks and bunkers.

quiz.q: Which part of the periscope is marked '?'
quiz.why: The top mirror turns incoming light down the tube.

quiz.q: Why can a submarine crew see above the water?
options: A periscope reflects light down to them twice
quiz.why: The periscope's two mirrors redirect light down to the viewer.

16.5.crux: Two mirrors placed at an angle make several images; a kaleidoscope uses three mirrors to make beautiful, ever-changing patterns.

cards.title: Mirrors at an angle

steps.text: Stand two mirrors at an angle, edges touching
Place a coin between them
You see several images of the coin

say: Light is reflected again and again between the two mirrors, so we see many images.
The smaller the angle between the mirrors, the more images you see.

cards.title: Making a kaleidoscope

steps.text: Join three rectangular mirror strips into a triangular tube (prism)
Put small pieces of coloured glass or bangles at one end
Look through the other end and rotate the tube

say: Repeated reflections turn a few coloured pieces into a beautiful pattern.
cards.remember: Kaleidoscope = three mirrors + coloured pieces + many reflections.

cards.title: Never the same twice

items.text: Every turn makes a new pattern

say: You'll never see exactly the same pattern again.

crux_points: Two mirrors at an angle produce several images.
A smaller angle gives more images.
A kaleidoscope uses three mirrors to make changing patterns.

quiz.q: How many mirrors does a kaleidoscope usually have?
quiz.why: Three mirror strips are joined into a prism shape.

quiz.q: Why do two inclined mirrors show many images?
options: Light reflects again and again between them
quiz.why: Repeated reflections create several images.

16.6.crux: White sunlight is a mix of seven colours; a prism splits it into these colours, which is called dispersion, and a rainbow is dispersion in nature.

cards.title: Splitting sunlight
say: A prism splits white light into a band of colours.
Splitting of light into its colours is called dispersion.

cards.title: Seven colours
say: Remember them with the word VIBGYOR.
cards.remember: VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

cards.title: Rainbows

steps.text: After rain, tiny water drops float in the air
Sunlight passes through the drops
Each drop acts like a prism and splits the light: a rainbow

say: You see a rainbow with the Sun behind you.

crux_points: White sunlight is made of seven colours.
A prism splits light into colours: dispersion.
A rainbow is dispersion of sunlight by raindrops.

quiz.q: Which colour is marked '?' (the one that bends most)?
quiz.why: Violet bends the most and appears at the bottom of the spectrum.

quiz.q: Splitting white light into its colours is called…
quiz.why: That's the definition of dispersion.

16.7.crux: Light enters the eye through the cornea and pupil, the lens focuses it on the retina, and the optic nerve carries the message to the brain.

cards.title: Parts of the eye

labels.name: Pupil
labels.note: The opening that lets light in

say: The eye is roughly round. Its tough white outer coat protects it.

cards.title: From light to sight

steps.text: Light passes through the cornea
It enters through the pupil (the iris adjusts its size)
The lens focuses it onto the retina
The optic nerve carries the signals to the brain

say: The iris makes the pupil small in bright light and large in dim light.
cards.remember: Cornea → pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve → brain.

cards.title: Rods and cones
say: The retina has two kinds of light-sensitive cells.
Owls have many rods and few cones, so they see well at night but poorly in daylight.

cards.title: Persistence of vision

steps.text: An image stays on the retina for about 1/16th of a second
Movies show about 24 pictures every second
So the pictures blend and we see smooth motion

say: This is why a quickly spinning fan looks like a disc.

crux_points: Light enters through the cornea and pupil; the iris controls the pupil's size.
The lens focuses light onto the retina, which has rods (dim light) and cones (colour).
The optic nerve carries signals to the brain; the blind spot has no sensory cells.

quiz.q: Which part is marked '?'
quiz.why: The lens, just behind the pupil, focuses light on the retina.

quiz.q: Owls see well at night because their eyes have…
quiz.why: Rods are sensitive to dim light.

quiz.q: Which part of the eye gives it its colour?
quiz.why: The iris is the coloured part of the eye.

16.8.crux: Look after your eyes: read in good light at a proper distance, never look at the Sun, don't rub them, eat food rich in vitamin A and get them checked.

cards.title: Good habits

items.sub: Not too dim, not too bright

say: Small habits protect your eyes for life.

cards.title: Never do this
say: Looking at the Sun or a very bright light can harm your eyes badly.

cards.title: Vitamin A
say: Too little vitamin A causes night blindness: difficulty seeing in dim light.

crux_points: Read in good light with the book about 25 cm away.
Never look at the Sun or rub your eyes; wash dust out with clean water.
Eat vitamin A rich foods to prevent night blindness; get regular check-ups.

quiz.q: Lack of which vitamin causes night blindness?
quiz.why: Vitamin A is needed for healthy eyes.

quiz.q: Dust has gone into your eye. What should you do?
quiz.why: Clean water washes the dust out safely; rubbing can hurt the eye.

16.9.crux: Visually impaired people sharpen their other senses and use aids, both non-optical (Braille, talking books, computers) and optical (magnifiers, special lenses), to read and write.

cards.title: Other senses
say: Some people are visually impaired from birth; others lose sight through disease or injury.
They develop their other senses more sharply.

cards.title: Helpful aids
say: Optical aids help people with low vision; non-optical aids help those who can't see at all.

cards.title: Inspiring people

items.sub: Are writers, musicians, teachers and scientists
By offering help politely and giving equal respect

say: With the right aids, visually impaired people can read, write and achieve a great deal.

crux_points: Visually impaired people rely more on hearing, touch and smell.
Non-optical aids include Braille, talking books and computers.
Optical aids include magnifiers and special lenses for low vision.

quiz.q: Which is a non-optical aid?
quiz.why: Talking books use sound, not sight.

quiz.q: Optical aids like magnifiers help people who…
quiz.why: They help people who still have some sight.

16.10.crux: Braille is a reading and writing system of raised dots, arranged in cells of six, that visually impaired people read with their fingertips.

cards.title: A Braille cell
say: Different patterns of raised dots stand for different letters, words and signs.
There are 63 dot patterns.

cards.title: Louis Braille

steps.text: Louis Braille lost his sight in an accident as a young child
He invented the dot system for visually impaired people
Nearly 200 years later, it is used all over the world

say: The system is named after him.
cards.remember: Braille: 6-dot cells, read with fingertips, invented by Louis Braille.

cards.title: How Braille is read

items.sub: Braille is used for many languages

say: Practised readers move their fingers smoothly along each line.

crux_points: Braille uses raised dots in cells of six.
There are 63 dot patterns for letters, words and signs.
It is read with the fingertips; invented by Louis Braille.

quiz.q: How many dot positions are there in one Braille cell?
quiz.why: Each cell has two columns of three dots.

quiz.q: Braille is read using…
quiz.why: The dots are raised so they can be felt.
